results.text: • BIRD[ 47] (BIg Bench for laRge-scale Database-grounded Text-to-SQL evaluation): a crossdomain benchmark designed to stress-test models on large, heterogeneous schemas and substantial data volumes. Here,cross-domainrefers to coverage of a wide variety of professional fields and database schemas, ranging from sports and finance to healthcare, blockchain, and education, so that evaluation is not biased toward any single domain. BIRD comprises 12,751 unique question–SQL pairs over 95 real-world databases totaling 33.4 GB of relational data, spanning 37 professional domains, and evaluates parser robustness against schema complexity, data scale, and domain variability. • UNITE[ 44] (A Unified Benchmark for Text-to-SQL Evaluation): UNITE assembles and normalizes eighteen public Text-to-SQL datasets into a single unified format to evaluate generalization across diverse schemas, SQL patterns, and domains.

ReViSQL (UIUC, March 2026).ReViSQL [100] is the first method to report human-level accuracy on BIRD, reaching 93.2% execution accuracy on an expert-verified BIRD Mini-Dev split and narrowly exceeding the 92.96% human-expert reference reported by the original benchmark. The paper’s central claim is methodological rather than architectural: it argues that the remaining gap between state-of-the-art agents and humans is driven by training-data quality rather than reasoning-pipeline design. To support this claim, the authors constructBIRD-Verified, a 2.5K-instance subset of the BIRD training set corrected through two to four rounds of independent review by SQL experts. They report annotation errors in 61.1% of the audited instances (52.1% in gold SQL queries, 26.2% in natural language questions, and 18.2% in external-knowledge fields), which is broadly consistent with concurrent findings on benchmark unreliability [39, 40].

Figure 4:Comparison of reward strategies for Text-to-SQL on BIRD. Each bar shows the execution accuracy reported in the original paper, together with the model size and reward design. Values are taken as reported and mix BIRD development and test splits, so they indicate broad trends rather than a controlled comparison. Moving from supervised cross-entropy (62.0%) to composite and execution-grounded rewards (up to 73.5%) suggests that fine-grained or verifiable reward functions yield substantial gains over supervised training alone, even at comparable model scales. outperforms larger proprietary systems on BIRD (e.g., o3-mini by about 4 points and Gemini-1.5-Pro-002 by about 3 points) and generalizes better than purely supervised baselines, with the largest gains on complex multi-table queries. SQL-R1.SQL-R1 [ 51] combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with GRPO to train a reasoningenhanced NL2SQL model.

Figure 3:Property coverage matrix for Text-to-SQL evaluation metrics. Each cell indicates whether a metric fully supports (∗), partially supports (o), or does not support (–) a given evaluation property. Execution Accuracy (EX) and Valid Efficiency Score (VES) require database access but capture semantic correctness, whereas structure-aware metrics such as SQAM and TSED provide partial credit and syntactic fidelity without requiring query execution, making them suitable for privacy-restricted or compliance-sensitive deployment settings. No single metric covers all properties, reinforcing the need for multi-metric evaluation protocols. 4.8 Challenges in Evaluation Although these metrics have helped standardize evaluation, each has limitations: • Exact match (EM)does not account for the syntactic flexibility of SQL and therefore penalizes queries that are logically correct but written in an alternative form.

Additional structure-oriented metrics used in practice include: • Component Matching (CM).Used in the Spider benchmark, CM breaks each SQL query into its main components, including SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY , ORDER BY , and keywords. For each component, it computes an F1 score between the predicted and ground-truth sets of sub-components while ignoring order. This enables fine-grained analysis of which parts of a query are generated correctly. • Exact Set Match (EM without values).Also used in Spider, this metric evaluates structural equivalence by treating the tables, columns, and operators within each clause as unordered sets and ignoring constant values. By focusing on structure rather than surface form, it credits semantically equivalent rewrites even when literal values differ. 13

results.text: 4.3 Evaluating Robustness via SQL2NL: Schema-Aligned Paraphrasing The SQL2NL framework [69] proposes a schema-aware approach to measure and improve therobustness of NL-to-SQL systems under lexical and syntactic variation. Rather than paraphrasing natural language questions naïvely (which can inadvertently change schema links), SQL2NL generates paraphrases conditioned on thegold SQLand the target database schema, producing diverse utterances that preserve the original intent while keeping schema alignment intact. This makes it possible to measure how sensitive a model is to wording, independently of schema-linking errors.

Key results.Experiments reveal substantial robustness deficits: large models exhibit notable executionaccuracy drops on paraphrases (around 10 percentage points for LLaMA-70B), and smaller models show even larger relative declines. results.text: Methodology.SQL2NL (i) ingests a gold SQL query and its schema description; (ii) prompts a generation model with constraints that encourage lexical and syntactic diversity while forbidding schemaidentifier leakage; (iii) validates paraphrase fidelity through automatic embedding-based checks and targeted human review of a sample; and (iv) evaluates NL-to-SQL systems by comparing execution accuracy on the original questions with that on the SQL2NL paraphrases. The framework supports weighted (human-adjusted) scoring so that low-quality paraphrases do not unduly penalize systems. SQL2NL can also produce augmented training data for robustness-oriented fine-tuning. Evaluation protocol and datasets.The authors apply SQL2NL to Spider and BIRD and stratify their analyses by query complexity (number of joins, nested clauses, and aggregates). The primary metrics are execution accuracyand therobustness gap, defined as the drop in execution accuracy from the original to the paraphrased questions.
